classification.difficultyReason: Identify and research wheel circumference and gearing alongside speed, connect distance per pedal revolution to cadence, and interpret comparisons between bicycles whose gearing may differ.

content.prompt: Research the linear speeds of a typical Olympic cyclist when doing the ‘hour record’. Using the techniques from Question 5, find how many revolutions per minute they were pedalling at (called the cadence), on average. Now research the typical speed of an average cyclist (or even yourself!) and compare.

answer.short: Answers vary. For speed $v$ km/h, wheel circumference $C$ metres and gear ratio $G$ (front teeth divided by rear teeth), cadence is $\frac{50v}{3CG}\text{ rpm}$. Speed alone does not determine cadence.
answer.worked:
For a fixed-gear bicycle rolling without slipping, let $v$ be speed in km/h, $C$ the wheel circumference in metres and $G$ the front-to-rear tooth ratio. One pedal revolution produces $G$ wheel revolutions, covering $CG$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}\text{distance per minute}&=\frac{1000v}{60}\text{ m}\\\text{cadence}&=\frac{1000v}{60CG}\\\text{cadence}&=\frac{50v}{3CG}\text{ rpm}.\end{align*}$$
Use each cyclist's speed, wheel circumference and gear ratio to calculate their cadence. Compare the two speeds and cadences. If both bicycles have the same circumference and gearing, their cadence ratio equals their speed ratio. Otherwise, compare the calculated cadences separately. There is no single numerical answer without the researched data.
